submission.summary:
Reviewed Harold Bennett's (pt-1008) apixaban dosing for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation against the FDA label dose-reduction criteria (2.5 mg BID if >=2 of: age >=80, weight <=60 kg, SCr >=1.5 mg/dL).

Findings:
- Age 81 (DOB 1945-02-20): MEETS
- Weight: 128.3 lb recorded at the 9/24/2026 post-hospital visit = 58.2 kg: MEETS. (The 9/28 pharmacy consult concluded he did not meet this criterion because it used the older 5/14/2026 flowsheet weight of 63.5 kg; the newer in-clinic weight, documented in pounds in the 9/24 progress note, shows ongoing weight loss below 60 kg.)
- Serum creatinine 1.31 mg/dL (9/24/2026, down from AKI peak 1.46): does NOT meet.

He meets 2 of 3 criteria, so the labeled dose is 2.5 mg twice daily. Changed apixaban from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily with the rationale documented in the order reason. No other medications were changed.

Suggested follow-up for the clinician: confirm the 9/24 weight on a repeat measurement and document it on the vitals flowsheet, and continue nutrition follow-up for ongoing weight loss, since the dose decision now rests on the weight criterion.

Reviewed Harold Bennett's (pt-1008) apixaban dosing against the FDA label for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation following his 9/24/2026 post-hospital visit labs.

Findings: Dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily is indicated when at least 2 of 3 criteria are met.
- Age >=80: MET (81 years, DOB 1945-02-20)
- Body weight <=60 kg: MET - 128.3 lb documented on the 9/24/2026 clinic scale = 58.2 kg. This weight was recorded in the progress note but not on the observation flowsheet, where the most recent value is still 63.5 kg from 5/14/2026. His trend supports it: 64.4 kg (12/2025) -> 63.5 kg (5/2026) -> 60.8 kg at 8/30 discharge -> 58.2 kg on 9/24, with ongoing poor appetite and weight loss noted.
- Serum creatinine >=1.5 mg/dL: NOT met (1.31 mg/dL on 9/24/2026)

2 of 3 criteria met, so the standing 5 mg twice daily dose was too high.

Action: Changed apixaban from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily, with the rationale documented in the change reason. No other medications were modified.

Note for the clinician: the 9/28/2026 pharmacy consult recommended continuing 5 mg BID based on the stale 5/14/2026 weight of 63.5 kg and therefore concluded only 1 of 3 criteria was met. Suggest adding the 9/24 weight to the flowsheet and informing the pharmacist/Dr. Okafor of this correction, and confirming the current weight at the next visit given the active weight-loss workup.

Reviewed Harold Bennett's (pt-1008) apixaban dosing for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation against the FDA label and corrected it.

FDA label criteria (reduce to 2.5 mg BID if >=2 of 3 present):
- Age >=80: MET — patient is 81 (DOB 1945-02-20).
- Body weight <=60 kg: MET — 128.3 lb (58.2 kg) measured on the clinic scale at the 9/24/2026 post-hospital visit.
- Serum creatinine >=1.5 mg/dL: NOT met — 1.31 mg/dL on 9/24/2026 (down from the AKI peak of 1.46 on 8/28; baseline ~1.25).

2 of 3 criteria are met, so apixaban was changed from 5 mg twice daily to 2.5 mg twice daily (med-1008-01).

Important discrepancy: the 9/28/2026 pharmacy consult concluded only 1 of 3 criteria were met and recommended continuing 5 mg BID, but it used the 5/14/2026 flowsheet weight of 63.5 kg. The more recent 9/24/2026 weight (58.2 kg) was documented only in the narrative of Dr. Okafor's progress note and was never entered into the vitals flowsheet, so it was missed. Given the ongoing documented weight loss (64.4 kg 12/2025 -> 63.5 kg 5/2026 -> 58.2 kg 9/2026) and poor appetite, the current weight is the appropriate value to use.

Recommended follow-up for the clinician: (1) enter the 9/24 weight into the vitals flowsheet so it is visible for future dosing checks, (2) confirm the weight at the next visit, and (3) note that if weight recovers above 60 kg with nutritional support while creatinine stays <1.5, the patient would revert to only 1 criterion and the 5 mg BID dose would again be correct.

No other medications were changed. No drug interactions (strong dual P-gp/CYP3A4 inhibitors) identified among metoprolol succinate ER, furosemide, and tamsulosin; no allergies on file.

Maria Lopez (pt-1003), seen 2026-10-01 with exudative pharyngitis, fever and positive rapid strep.

Key safety finding: Her allergy list contained only "sulfonamide antibiotics (rash)," but the 2019 outside ED note (Valley General, note-1003-1) documents that she had hives with lip and throat swelling ~30 minutes after a dose of Augmentin, treated with epinephrine — i.e., a prior anaphylactic reaction to a penicillin. This had never been coded on the allergy list, so first-line amoxicillin/penicillin would have been a serious hazard.

Actions taken:
1. Added allergy: Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate/Augmentin), reaction anaphylaxis, criticality high, category medication, with source noted.
2. Prescribed azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 3 days for Group A strep pharyngitis — a guideline-accepted non–beta-lactam alternative. Cephalexin was deliberately avoided: with a history of true anaphylaxis (and aminopenicillin side-chain similarity to first-generation cephalosporins), a cephalosporin is not appropriate without allergy evaluation. Clindamycin is an equally acceptable alternative if a macrolide is undesirable. No interaction with her amlodipine or atorvastatin; no other QT-prolonging agents on her list.

Suggestions for the clinician: consider adding an acute pharyngitis/GAS code to the problem list (no tool available to me for that), and consider referral for formal penicillin allergy evaluation, since a confirmed or delabeled penicillin allergy will affect future antibiotic choices.

Maria Lopez (pt-1003) — GAS pharyngitis with positive rapid strep (Dr. Shah urgent visit note 2026-10-01).

KEY SAFETY FINDING: Her active allergy list contained only "sulfonamide antibiotics (rash)," but the 2019 outside ED note (Valley General, note-1003-1) documents a history of ANAPHYLAXIS to Augmentin — hives with lip and throat swelling ~30 minutes after a dose, treated with epinephrine. First-line amoxicillin/penicillin would have been unsafe, and cephalosporins are also best avoided given the anaphylactic (not merely rash) phenotype.

Actions taken:
1. Added allergy: Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate/Augmentin), reaction anaphylaxis, criticality HIGH, category medication — so the allergy fires on future orders.
2. Prescribed azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 5 days for GAS pharyngitis — an IDSA-endorsed non-beta-lactam alternative for patients with severe/anaphylactic penicillin allergy. No interaction with her amlodipine or atorvastatin (clarithromycin was avoided for that reason; clindamycin 300 mg TID x10 days is the backup if she cannot tolerate a macrolide or fails to improve).

No changes made to amlodipine or atorvastatin. Note for the clinician: please confirm the penicillin allergy history directly with the patient at follow-up, and counsel that local macrolide resistance in GAS means she should return if not improving after 48 hours, as already outlined in the visit note.

Maria Lopez (pt-1003) — Group A strep pharyngitis, rapid strep positive (Dr. Shah urgent visit note 2026-10-01).

Key finding: Her active allergy list contained only "sulfonamide antibiotics." However, the outside ED note from 2019-08-12 documents a patient-reported ANAPHYLACTIC reaction to Augmentin (hives with lip and throat swelling ~30 min post-dose, treated with epinephrine). This had never been added to the coded allergy list, so a penicillin/amoxicillin order — the usual first-line therapy for strep pharyngitis — would have been placed without any safety warning.

Actions taken:
1. Added allergy: Penicillins (amoxicillin-clavulanate / Augmentin), reaction anaphylaxis, criticality HIGH, category medication, with the source of the history noted.
2. Prescribed azithromycin 500 mg PO once daily x 5 days for GAS pharyngitis.

Rationale for drug choice: Amoxicillin/penicillin V contraindicated by the anaphylaxis history. Cephalexin was avoided because the reaction was a true IgE-mediated anaphylaxis rather than a mild rash. Sulfonamides are excluded by her existing allergy (and are not appropriate for GAS). Azithromycin is a guideline-recommended alternative for penicillin-allergic patients and was preferred over clarithromycin, which has significant CYP3A4 interactions with her amlodipine and atorvastatin; clindamycin was a reasonable alternative but azithromycin was chosen for tolerability and simpler dosing. No interaction concerns with azithromycin and her current amlodipine/atorvastatin.

Note for the ordering clinician: local macrolide resistance in GAS is variable — if she is not improving after 48 hours of therapy, consider switching to clindamycin and/or obtaining a throat culture with susceptibilities.
